title: The Creature No One Can Tame
overview: God keeps answering Job by describing Leviathan, a terrifying sea creature no human can catch or control, to show that only the one who made it is truly in charge.

parts.label: You cannot catch it (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: God fires questions at Job: can he hook Leviathan like a fish, make it beg for mercy, keep it as a pet or sell it at market? The answer to each is obviously no, and anyone who tries once will never try again.

parts.label: Then who can face me? (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: If no one dares to stir up this creature, no one can put its Maker on trial, as Job has wanted to do. God owes nobody anything, because everything under heaven already belongs to him.

parts.label: Armor and teeth (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: God now praises the creature's strength and even its beauty, from its terrifying jaws to its back of overlapping scales like shields. The scales fit so tightly that not even air gets through, so no weapon can either.

parts.label: Fire and smoke (vv. 18-21)
parts.note: Its snorting flashes light, and smoke and flames come from its mouth and nose. This may be poetic exaggeration of a real animal's spray glinting in the sun, or it may draw on old dragon imagery, and scholars are unsure which.

parts.label: Weapons are useless (vv. 22-29)
parts.note: Terror runs ahead of it, and even strong warriors fall back when it rises. Swords, spears, arrows, sling stones and clubs bounce off as if they were straw.

parts.label: King of the proud (vv. 30-34)
parts.note: Its sharp underside scores the mud like a threshing sledge, a heavy board studded with stones that was dragged over grain, and it churns the sea into white foam behind it. Nothing on earth matches it, yet the whole speech has made clear that it is still God's creature.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Leviathan is a real animal described in poetry, such as a crocodile or whale, or a symbol of chaos drawn from ancient sea monster stories, which shifts whether the point is God's power over nature or over every force of disorder.
think: When you meet something far bigger and wilder than you could ever control, does it make you feel smaller, safer, or something else entirely?
